Through the consciousness of the author of a Phenomenology, humanity itself is, so to speak, remembering its past and trying to understand how and why it became what it is at this particular historical moment.
Yet the “conception” of the historical present given by a Phenomenology can never be completely exhaustive.

Phenomenology is, if one likes, “autobiographical” and therefore “subjective” in the sense that it does not show what humanity’s past really was. It shows only how that past appeared to humanity in the course of its history and how it appears to humanity at the historical moment in question.
Phenomenology therefore describes the historical sequence of the ways in which human beings appear to human beings—that is, to themselves.

But because these appearances appear to a human being, and therefore to the very kind of being that carries out the historical process, the sequence of appearances reproduces the sequence of historical events themselves, both chronologically and dialectically.
We can therefore say that a Phenomenology is nothing other than a description of the autobiographical aspect of the universal history of humanity.
If Phenomenology can be defined as a phenomenological autobiography, we must not forget that its main purpose is not simply, or even mainly, to describe its author philosophically.
Its purpose is to transform its author, through that very description, from a non-philosopher into a philosopher—that is, into someone capable of writing a complete philosophical system.

Phenomenology must therefore be “true” in more than the ordinary scientific sense, according to which the meaning of its descriptions must correspond exactly to the real content of the object described.

It must also be true in the strong sense, because it is the necessary premise of truth in that strong sense: of definitive, complete, and exhaustive knowledge of the most concrete reality—of “perfect” knowledge, or omniscience.
As we already know, the philosophical system in the strict sense—that is, Cosmology and Ontology—gives a complete answer to the following question:
What must the existing world, and the being underlying it, be like for it to be able to “appear” to human beings exactly as it actually does?
Since the answer must be definitive and therefore exhaustive, it necessarily presupposes complete knowledge of all appearances or phenomena.
That is precisely the kind of knowledge Phenomenology is, in principle, supposed to provide.
Phenomenological description must therefore be not only correct, but also complete.
On the one hand, Phenomenology must give a correct—that is, exact and exhaustive—description of each individual appearance.
On the other hand, it must describe in this way all appearances that exist, or more precisely, all essentially distinct types of appearance.
In other words, the content of Phenomenology must be true in the strong, philosophical sense.
The knowledge of phenomena that it provides must, as people say, be universal and necessary.

The universality of Phenomenology means that anyone capable of understanding its content must find that content convincing. Anyone who understands it must necessarily agree with what its author says and make the author’s discourse their own.
The necessity of Phenomenology means that neither its author nor anyone else can alter its content in any way.
Nothing can be added to it.
Nothing can be removed from it.
And everything said in the Phenomenology must be said exactly as it is said.
This also means that the knowledge it offers is definitive or perfect—true in the strong sense of the word.
It is true both because each individual description is correct, exact, and exhaustive, and because it describes everything that can in principle be described.
In this sense, phenomenological knowledge has a philosophical character.

And since philosophical knowledge is “perfect” knowledge or omniscience, not only because it is knowledge of everything but because it includes all true knowledge whatsoever, it follows that knowing that philosophical knowledge is true—that it is omniscience—is itself part of philosophical knowledge.
Philosophy must itself show, to itself and to others, that its descriptions are “universal and necessary”—that is, true in the strong sense, or more exactly, exhaustive and all-embracing.
And insofar as Phenomenology itself has a philosophical character, it must do the same with its own descriptions.
Admittedly, its descriptions cannot be called fully exhaustive, since Phenomenology describes not the most concrete reality itself but only its appearances, its phenomenological aspect.
But within that aspect, its descriptions must be just as exact, exhaustive, and complete as a philosophical description of reality itself.
Phenomenology must therefore itself demonstrate both this exactness and completeness and the fact that its description of phenomena must be supplemented by a description of the reality that appears.
Only by doing this can it become what it is above all meant to be: a dialectical introduction to philosophy.

Once it has described all phenomena exactly and exhaustively, it shows, first, why the philosophical question in the strict sense must be asked—the question of the “cause” of those phenomena. And second, it gives the philosopher the means to answer that question exhaustively.

How, then—by what “method”—can Phenomenology show, on the one hand, that its descriptions are exact and exhaustive and, on the other, prove that the work itself is genuinely complete, that it describes all phenomena?
We know that, for Hegel, philosophy can prove its own truth only because, in being true, it is also circular.
And we already know what this circularity means: philosophy returns to its point of departure and repeats what it has already passed through.
In principle, philosophical “circularity” can begin anywhere.

What matters is that, after beginning with the description of some particular appearance—or some “element,” “moment,” or “stage” of reality—philosophy must pass necessarily and universally to the description of another.
And this other element is precisely determined. From A, one must necessarily and universally pass to B; one cannot pass directly to C, D, E, and so on, at least not without first passing through B.
By moving from one description to another in this way, philosophy finally returns to the description with which it began.
If we wish to continue, all we can do is trace the same circle again, indefinitely. Having gone from Z to A, we must once again go from A to B, then from B to C, and so on until Z; then begin again.
This circular structure genuinely guarantees the absolute truth of philosophy.

First, it shows that the description has exhausted all possibilities. Nothing can be added to what has been said, because every possible movement forward or beyond it remains inside the tightly closed circle.
Second, circularity guarantees the validity of each individual description.

To begin with, each description is exhaustive. If it were not, there would be no necessity to move on to another description. Only a complete description of an appearance can reveal its incompleteness and therefore the need to supplement it with a new description. So nothing can be removed from any given description.
And second, the descriptions are exact. If they were not, the movement of description would, so to speak, go astray and fail to return to its starting point. So nothing in them can be altered.
A circular philosophy is therefore necessarily true, and a true philosophy is necessarily circular—insofar as it is clear that only philosophy can be true in this strong sense.
And it is easy to see that this circularity of true philosophy is nothing other than what we previously called its dialectical character.
If the transition from one description to another is neither accidental nor arbitrary, but “necessary and universal,” then this means that the transition is determined by the reality being described.
We must pass from description A to description B because A itself passes into B.
And this necessary real transition is nothing other than real dialectic in the proper sense: the dialectical process through which reality becomes what it becomes.
It is therefore just as inappropriate to speak of a philosophical “circular method” as it is to speak of a “dialectical” or ***a posteriori* deductive method**.
The method of philosophy is always and everywhere the same: pure description.
If this description takes on a dialectical character, that is only because—as we already know—the reality being described is itself dialectical.
For exactly the same reason, philosophical description also turns out to be ***a posteriori* deductive**.
Dialectical reality itself is necessarily “genetic” and, if one likes, “deductive”: it “constructs” or “deduces” itself from its “initial” state.
And for precisely the same reason, philosophical description is circular.
It is circular because dialectical reality itself is necessarily circular.
In one sense, every dialectical triad is circular, since synthesis preserves the thesis and therefore, in a certain way, “returns” to it.
And in the strong sense, the entire real dialectical process is circular.
So the closed circle of philosophy is nothing other than the pure description of the closed circle of real dialectic—that is, of the universal history of humanity.
It is true that Phenomenology, in the sense just described, is not fully circular.

When it “ends”—when its descriptions reach their conclusion—it does not simply send author and reader back to the beginning. Instead, it carries them further, toward becoming philosophers in the strict sense: people whose task is now to describe the “causes” of the phenomena described by Phenomenology, that is, their existing and operative conditions of possibility.
Phenomenology examines phenomena and nothing but phenomena: the way the natural and historical world appears to human beings.
In other words, it presupposes the existence of human beings and excludes from its description anything that exists, in some sense, before humanity.

In this respect, the animal that first gave rise to human existence, and the natural world that necessarily provided the conditions for that animal’s life, lie outside the limits of what phenomenological description can reach.
Yet Phenomenology must in one way or another know about this animal.
And this knowledge functions for Phenomenology as an axiom: if not something that must be proved, then at least something that cannot be proved from within Phenomenology itself.
So when Phenomenology reaches its end and returns to this “axiomatic” starting point, it directs its author and reader toward philosophy proper, where the axiom itself must be “proved.”
Only the system of knowledge as a whole, therefore, is fully circular, because it includes both Phenomenology and Philosophy proper.
The complete system is genuinely closed and self-sufficient.
It contains no “axiom” or premise borrowed from outside itself.
It therefore needs no supplement from some essentially different kind of knowledge.
It derives all its own conclusions and “proves” or “deduces” all its own premises.

If some “given” serves as its starting point—a given that initially appears contingent and unprovable—then because the completed system necessarily returns to its starting point, that starting point becomes at the same time the system’s end.
The beginning therefore turns out to be the result of the system’s own deductions and hence a “necessary” and “demonstrated” effect.
Taken as a whole, the system therefore “proves”—that is, guarantees the truth, necessity, and universality—of every one of its parts.
Nothing in it is simply “accepted on faith,” and nothing remains incapable of being completely explained—that is, explained in all its consequences.
In the strong sense, the individual parts of the system cannot themselves be called fully circular.

Neither Phenomenology nor Philosophy, nor the two parts of Philosophy—Ontology and Cosmology—are fully circular. Nor are the sections of Cosmology, one of which describes nature and the other humanity.
Ontology has no premises, but it produces deductions or consequences that go beyond its own limits. The other parts of the system have both premises and consequences.
Even so, all the fundamental parts of the system are “circular” in the sense that each returns to its own starting point.
And it is only by returning to that starting point that each passes beyond its own limits.
Thus Phenomenology, after making a complete circuit of phenomenological description, passes into Philosophy and finally, more specifically, into Ontology.
How does Phenomenology achieve this circularity that guarantees its truth?
As I have already said, it does not achieve it by means of some special “circular method.”
